kept.claim: When the cached map denies a new (name, parent), Check always runs a fresh permission-store query (getUserPermissions no longer reads permCache; singleflight only merges concurrent calls), so N distinct denied resources for one user/action cost up to N queries per 30s instead of 1. In-proc, this adds to the loss of the client-side cache. It is probably a deliberate freshness trade-off, and a per-(user, action) requery limit is a hardening suggestion rather than a fix for a proven regression.
kept.body:
## [OPTIMIZATION] A cached deny always triggers a fresh permission-store query; consider limiting requeries per (user, action)

**Severity:** LOW — More DB load for denied Checks; the hot List/Compile paths are not affected

### The Problem

```go
cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)
if err == nil {
    allowed, err := s.checkPermission(ctx, cachedPerms, checkReq)
    ...
    if allowed { return ... }       // only an allow short-circuits
}
permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)   // line 139
```

`getUserPermissions` no longer reads `permCache` (the read at old lines 316-320 was removed), so each cached deny for a `(name, parent)` not seen before runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions`. `sf.Do` only merges *concurrent* calls. `permDenialCache` only helps when the *same* `(name, parent)` is checked again. Team and basic-role lookups are still cached, so the extra cost is one permission SQL query per new denied resource.

### Theory / Proof

Before the PR, one cached map per `(user, action)` answered every Check for 30s. Now a user who requests N different resources they can't access within 30s causes up to N permission queries. In-proc, this comes on top of dropping the authlib client-side check cache (`NoopCache`, rbac.go:101-105).

### What happens today vs. what will break

This looks like a deliberate trade-off: re-fetching after a deny is what makes newly granted access work right away. The main list and bulk paths use `List`/`Compile`, which still serve from the cached map (service.go:180-192), and Check is called once per API request. So the extra load grows with how many different denied resources users request (scanners, bots, users following stale links), not with page size.

### Recommendation

To cap the worst case, limit requeries per `(user, action)` with a short marker that is set whenever `getUserPermissions` runs:

```go
if !allowed {
    refreshKey := userPermCacheKey(ns.Value, uid, action) + "_refreshed"
    if _, recent := s.permRefreshCache.Get(ctx, refreshKey); recent { // e.g. 5s TTL
        s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)
        return deny, nil
    }
}
```

With this, a burst of denied Checks costs at most one DB query per `(user, action)` every few seconds, and new grants still show up quickly.
kept.evidence: service.go:116-137 falls through to getIdentityPermissions after a cached deny; getUserPermissions (service.go:370-412) no longer reads permCache, so it always runs permissionStore.GetUserPermissions; singleflight only merges concurrent calls. Team/basic-role lookups are still cached. List/Compile paths (resource/server.go:719,823; bulk.go:166) still use the cached map, and Check is called once per request (apiserver/auth/authorizer/resource.go:31; folders/authorizer.go:87), so the N-query cost needs N separate requests for different denied resources. Looks like a deliberate freshness trade-off.

kept.claim: The fallback re-fetches permissions but not the 30s-cached folder tree, so a deny caused by a stale folderCache (e.g. a dashboard or folder just moved or created under a folder the user can access) is written to permDenialCache and pinned for another 30s, about 60s worst case versus <=30s before.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] Denial cache can pin a deny that came from a stale folder tree

**Severity:** LOW — Inherited-folder access can take up to about 60s to appear, versus <=30s before

### The Problem

```go
if !allowed {
    s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)   // 30s TTL
}
```

The requery path refreshes the permission map, but `checkInheritedPermissions` still uses `buildFolderTree`, which returns the 30s `folderCache` without refreshing it (service.go:613-616). Take a dashboard or subfolder that was just created in (or moved to) a folder the user has access to, where the user has no direct grant on the item. The cached tree doesn't know the new parent chain yet, so `tree.Ancestors(req.ParentFolder)` returns nothing, and the fresh map still denies. That deny is then cached under `(user, action, name, parent)`.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Before the PR, a deny caused by a stale tree ended once `folderCache` expired (<=30s), because every Check re-read the tree. Now a deny computed just before the tree expires is held in `permDenialCache` for another 30s, for a total of about 60s. For the plain deny-then-grant case the PR does not make things worse, because denials are only cached right after a fresh DB fetch.

### Recommendation

Don't cache a deny that depended on inherited-folder evaluation, or rebuild the tree before caching it:

```go
if !allowed && checkReq.ParentFolder == "" {
    s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)
}
```

Alternatively, give denials a shorter TTL than the folder tree (e.g. 5-10s) so the two staleness windows don't add up.
kept.evidence: Deny-then-grant is not a regression: before the PR, permCache was already 30s, and denials are only cached right after a fresh DB fetch (service.go:139-155), so the upper bound is the same. The regression holds only for inherited folder permissions: buildFolderTree returns the 30s folderCache without refreshing it (service.go:613-616), so a deny caused by a stale tree can be pinned in permDenialCache for another 30s (worst case about 60s vs <=30s before).

kept.claim: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_', which Grafana UIDs can contain, so a denial for dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' also denies dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c'.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] Denial cache key is ambiguous because `_` is a legal UID character

**Severity:** LOW — Wrong denies (not escalation) for resources whose UID/folder UID contain underscores

### The Problem

```go
func userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent string) string {
    return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent
}
```

- `name="a",   parent="b_c"` -> `...dashboards:read_a_b_c`
- `name="a_b", parent="c"`   -> `...dashboards:read_a_b_c`

These are the same key. If the first Check is denied, the second resource is also denied for 30s without being evaluated, even when the user has access to it.

### Theory / Proof

Grafana UIDs allow `[a-zA-Z0-9\-_]` (see `util.IsValidShortUID`), and many provisioned or imported dashboards use underscores. The denial cache is checked before any permission evaluation (service.go:116-121), so a colliding key directly produces `Allowed: false`.

### What happens today vs. what will break

The error only goes toward denying, so it is not a security hole. It is a correctness bug that is hard to diagnose: access flips depending on which resource was checked first.

### Recommendation

Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode the parts:

```go
func userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent string) string {
    return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "/" + parent
}
```

(`/` is not a valid UID character). A length-prefixed or `%q`-quoted format also works.
kept.evidence: cache.go:30-32 joins parts with '_' and no escaping; pkg/util/shortid_generator.go:33-34 allows '_' in UIDs; name 'a'+folder 'b_c' and name 'a_b'+folder 'c' produce the same key; service.go:116-121 returns Allowed=false before any evaluation.

kept.claim: The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test passes even if the denial cache is removed, because the cached map sets dash1 to false and the fake store returns no permissions, so it does not test the short-circuit.
kept.body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] Denial-cache test cannot fail if the denial cache is broken

**Severity:** LOW — The new denial-cache short-circuit has no real test coverage

### The Problem

```go
// Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked
s.permCache.Set(ctx, userPermCacheKey(...), map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false})
```

The comment says it grants access, but the value is `false`, so `checkPermission` denies. The fallback then calls the `fakeStore` from `setupService()`, whose `userPermissions` is nil, so the DB path also denies. The test asserts `Allowed == false`, and that result happens whether or not `permDenialCache` exists.

### What happens today vs. what will break

If someone later removes or breaks the denial-cache lookup (for example, a key mismatch between Get and Set), this test still passes.

### Recommendation

Make both the cache and the store grant access, and assert that the store was not called:

```go
fStore := &fakeStore{userID: userID, userPermissions: []accesscontrol.Permission{{Action: "dashboards:read", Scope: "dashboards:uid:dash1"}}}
s.store, s.permissionStore = fStore, fStore
s.permCache.Set(ctx, userPermCacheKey("org-12", "test-uid", "dashboards:read"), map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true})
...
assert.False(t, resp.Allowed)
assert.Equal(t, 0, fStore.calls)
```

Also add a test that a denied Check writes the denial entry, so that Get/Set key symmetry is covered.
kept.evidence: Traced with the denial-cache block removed: the cached map {dash1:false} gives deny; fakeStore.ListFolders returns nil, so the inherited check is false; the DB fallback has nil basicRole/teams/perms, so the result is deny. The test passes either way.
